# THE OMNIMASTER HANDBOOK
## A technical autobiography told through systems, failures, decisions and working code

**Cayelaem Jantjies | Data Engineering · Analytics · Full-Stack Development · Applied AI · Platform Engineering**  
**Edition 01 | 9 November 2026 | Johannesburg, South Africa**

[Back to my GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Interactive portfolio](https://omnimaster-portfolio.onrender.com) · [Professional project atlas](PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md)

---

> I started with statistics and reports. The questions grew: Where did that number come from? Why did the pipeline fail? Who is authorised to see it? What happens when the database changes while somebody is using the application? Eventually the answer could not fit inside a dashboard. It had to become a system.

This handbook is the long-form companion to my GitHub profile. It is not a generic tech stack dump, a collection of AI-written product claims or a claim to have mastered every platform. Think of it as an open engineering notebook about **who I am, what I have built, how I think, what has gone wrong, how I investigate it, and where I want to go**.

**Continue to [Volume II: The OmniMaster Field Guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md)** for architecture diagrams, debugging casebooks, worked engineering exercises, a role-to-evidence navigator and six decision records. Volume I is the narrative; Volume II is the engineer's desk.

**Study or meet the human:** [Volume III · OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) teaches the skills with exercises and capstones.

**Learn how I design for people:** [Volume VI · The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) covers UI/UX development, usability, inclusive interface systems and real product design trade-offs.

**Build a real teaching project:** [Volume V · Build a System With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) teaches a complete synthetic data-to-decision system, with replay, rollback, reconciliation and tests. The [30-day expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) turns those skills into daily practice.
 [Volume IV · The Person Behind the Code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) explains my self-described INTJ habits, systems mindset, collaboration style and IT range. [The Arcade](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md) adds executable detective scenarios.

## The four boundaries of my engineering work

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Understand the source"] --> B["Engineer reliable data"]
    B --> C["Deliver useful decisions"]
    C --> D["Operate and protect"]
    D -->|"feedback, incidents and learning"| A
~~~

A query is not finished because it returns rows. A dashboard is not finished because it has a colour palette. An API is not finished because it returns 200. A model is not finished because its answer sounds plausible. I focus on the boundary **between correct code and useful, trustworthy software**.

## How to read the evidence

Every project or statement should be read with its delivery status:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Professional delivery** | Historical engagement or responsibility described in my CV and professional record; private source code may not be shareable |
| **Public implementation** | Source is visible in a linked repository; this does not automatically mean deployed or secure |
| **Prototype / synthetic demonstration** | Works with fictional data or limited features; no customer production claim |
| **Staging / active development** | Implemented work or candidate release with outstanding verification or rollout gates |
| **Design direction** | Proposed architecture or product outcome, not evidence that it shipped |
| **CV-reported metric** | Outcome from my professional record, not independently rerun in a public benchmark |

The most important rule: **a PR is not a deployed feature, a passing unit test is not a security certification, and a planned public-sector integration is not a government contract**.

# THE OMNIMASTER FIELD GUIDE
### Volume II of my living engineering textbook

**Cayelaem Jantjies · Engineering architectures, investigations, working exercises and technical conversations · November 2026**

[← Return to the main handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [GitHub profile](../README.md) · [Runnable labs](../projects/README.md)

---

> The main handbook explains where I came from and the systems I work on. This volume opens the engine room: the boundaries, choices, breakages and practical questions that shape my approach.

This is a companion to my ten-chapter [OmniMaster Handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md). Read it as an engineering field manual and an invitation to inspect my thinking.

## Start where your curiosity leads

| Reader | Starting point | What you'll discover |
|---|---|---|
| **Recruiter or hiring manager** | [04 · Role and evidence navigator](field-guide/04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md) | My experience, roles I fit, concrete project references and honest limitations |
| **Data engineer / architect** | [01 · Annotated architecture atlas](field-guide/01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) | End-to-end boundaries, CDC, semantics, AI and security |
| **Senior engineer / reviewer** | [02 · The debugging casebook](field-guide/02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md) | Failure symptoms, competing hypotheses, investigations and safe fixes |
| **Interview panel** | [03 · Engineering workbook](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md) | Worked problem-solving scenarios, tests and discussion prompts |
| **Technical lead** | [05 · Architecture decision journal](field-guide/05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md) | Trade-offs, alternatives, decision criteria and release evidence |

## Volume II chapters

1. [**Architecture atlas:** trace systems from operational truth to user outcome](field-guide/01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md)
2. [**Debugging casebook:** how I investigate things that break](field-guide/02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md)
3. [**Engineering workbook:** exercises, answers and reproducible code](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md)
4. [**Role and evidence map:** a guided tour for a recruiter or technical leader](field-guide/04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md)
5. [**Decision journal:** design records and the trade-offs they expose](field-guide/05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md)

## The central system question

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["People & business problem"] --> S["Source facts & constraints"]
    S --> E["Engineering decision"]
    E --> I["Implementation"]
    I --> V["Evidence & tests"]
    V --> O["Operating outcome"]
    O -->|"new information"| P
~~~

A strong engineer can move around this loop in either direction. From a failed KPI, trace the measure back to source records. From a security flaw, find the trust boundary. From an attractive product proposal, isolate the business event and the operating cost.

I want these materials to show **how I reason**, not invent achievements. Where a client record cannot be published, I use an explicitly hypothetical illustration. Where the public code contains unfinished work, I name the issue or pull request instead of claiming release success.

## Companion volumes and evidence

- **Volume I:** [The OmniMaster Handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md), the career narrative and ten technical chapters.
- **Volume III:** [The OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md), seven study modules and capstone blueprints.
- **Volume IV:** [The Person Behind the Code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md), INTJ as self-description and my approach to working across IT.
- **Arcade:** [The OmniMaster Arcade](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md), learning puzzles and a runnable incident game.
- **Volume V:** [Build a System With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md), six guided lessons and a runnable end-to-end synthetic data platform.
- **Volume VI:** [The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md), UI/UX development, accessibility, human research and measurable usability.
- **Daily practice:** [30-Day Engineering Expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) and [offline interactive study room](interactive/index.html).
- **Source archive:** [Project portfolio atlas](PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md) and [real-world mission dossiers](OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md).
- **Professional engagements:** [Client case studies](CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md), subject to appropriate confidentiality.
- **Code you can run:** [Four synthetic engineering labs](../projects/README.md), with tests and CI.
- **Live engineering issues:** [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues) and [Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/issues), where some work is intentionally not declared complete.

**Evidence standard:** a design diagram is not proof of deployment. A scenario is not a disclosed client incident. A green unit test is not an operational acceptance test. A career metric from my CV is reported history, not a new benchmark.

[Begin with the architecture atlas →](field-guide/01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md)

# THE OMNIMASTER ACADEMY
### Volume III | Learn the engineering habits, build the systems, and explain the decisions

**A practical study guide by Cayelaem Jantjies · November 2026**  
[GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Volume I: My story](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Volume II: Field guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [The person behind the code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md)

---

> Don't copy my job titles. Copy the process: understand the business event, reproduce the bug, model the facts, build the workflow, test the boundaries, and explain the trade-offs.

This is the part of my GitHub where I try to make myself *replaceable in the best possible way*: anyone who is curious and willing to practise should be able to follow the same engineering principles. It doesn't promise you my career or turn six weeks of tutorials into a senior engineer. It gives you a route from a blank repository to a defensible project.

**Who it's for:** a student, career-switcher, BI analyst moving toward engineering, software developer learning data, or engineer curious about applied AI and delivery.

**Cost and access:** the main exercises use Python, SQLite, Git and a code editor. They're designed to run locally with synthetic data, without an AWS account, paid AI API or work-owned credentials.

## Pick a route

| Track | Best for | Start |
|---|---|---|
| **New to engineering** | Build foundations one boundary at a time | [01 · Learn how to learn](academy/01_START_HERE.md) |
| **Already working in BI** | Move upstream to SQL, pipelines, contracts and APIs | [02 · The data model](academy/02_SQL_AND_MODELLING.md) |
| **Already building apps** | Make data and access boundaries trustworthy | [04 · Full-stack workflows](academy/04_BUILD_APPLICATIONS.md) |
| **Curious about applied AI** | Add models to workflows without trusting unvalidated output | [05 · Applied AI with guardrails](academy/05_APPLIED_AI.md) |
| **Preparing for senior interviews** | Prove understanding through negative tests and release criteria | [06 · Security and delivery](academy/06_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md) |
| **Want a portfolio piece** | Build and explain an entire system | [07 · Capstones and evidence](academy/07_CAPSTONES.md) |

## The seven modules

1. [**01. Think like an investigator:** define the problem, tools and learning journal](academy/01_START_HERE.md)
2. [**02. SQL and modelling:** business grain, joins, measures, indexing and tests](academy/02_SQL_AND_MODELLING.md)
3. [**03. Reliable data movement:** ingestion, quality, CDC, retries and history](academy/03_PIPELINES_AND_CDC.md)
4. [**04. Full-stack engineering:** APIs, state transitions, tenant scope and UI](academy/04_BUILD_APPLICATIONS.md)
5. [**05. Applied AI responsibly:** evidence, evaluation, costs and human review](academy/05_APPLIED_AI.md)
6. [**06. Security, testing and release:** negative paths, CI and rollback](academy/06_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md)
7. [**07. Capstones:** combine the layers into a real portfolio narrative](academy/07_CAPSTONES.md)

## A suggested 12-week route

| Weeks | Focus | Minimum evidence you should produce |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Tools, data grain, SQL and modelling | A reproducible source table, schema, query tests and explanation |
| 3–4 | Ingestion, contracts, state changes and replay | Synthetic ETL/CDC simulation, duplicate/deletion tests and failure diary |
| 5–6 | API + database + minimal interface | Authenticated CRUD-style workflow, tests, schema and clear error behaviour |
| 7–8 | Applied AI and risk assessment | Offline evaluator, test cases, human-review logic and explicit no-model fallback |
| 9–10 | CI, secrets, release rehearsal | Automated tests, negative cases, restore/rollback document |
| 11–12 | One capstone and evidence-led communication | README, architecture diagram, demo steps, trade-offs, what failed, what's next |

This is a **suggested study cadence**, not a promise of completion or a qualification. Repeat any module until you can explain it without copying an answer.

## How to measure learning

Use **evidence**, not hours of videos watched. At the end of a module, ask:

1. Can I reproduce the behaviour from clean inputs?
2. Can I explain why the design has this grain and these boundaries?
3. Which failure case did I intentionally create?
4. Can a stranger run the test without my machine or credentials?
5. What remains unproved, and how would I verify it in production?

Write one short engineering journal entry after each module: **problem → hypothesis → experiment → result → decision → remaining risk**.

## Practice repository

Start with the four [public engineering labs](../projects/README.md). They include a CDC replay, data quality contracts, SQL query plans and a synthetic source-grounding evaluator. Next, play the [OmniMaster Incident Academy game](../projects/omnimaster-incident-academy/) to practise reasoning about failure modes.

For worked explanations and reviewer questions, use the [Volume II workbook](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md). For the story behind these habits, read [Why I work this way](personal/02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md).

## The rules of this classroom

- Never paste employer data, production secrets or real learner/customer records into a tutorial.
- Do not present a lab as a production CDC service, live AI system or security certification.
- Prefer a boring correct solution to an impressive untestable one.
- Record what you couldn't solve. That is how a useful engineering notebook starts.
- Learning a language is not the same thing as understanding its underlying system.

**Graduation means you have a project that another engineer can question, run and improve.** There is no imaginary certificate. Your source, tests and explanations are the credential.

## Go beyond the course

[**Volume V: Build a System With Me**](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) supplies a complete fictional SQLite pipeline with six guided engineering chapters, replay and failure tests. [The 30-day expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) turns the syllabus into daily artifacts. For a more playful format, open the [live interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) in any browser.


[Start lesson 01 →](academy/01_START_HERE.md) · [Try the arcade →](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md)


**Design for people:** [Volume VI](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) adds a six-chapter UI/UX development and usability course.


### Read lessons without opening GitHub

The [live OmniMaster Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) serves all Academy lessons directly as readable HTML. The [frontend/backend book](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/OMNIMASTER_FULLSTACK_PLAYBOOK.md) and its [PDF edition](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/downloads/omnimaster-fullstack.pdf) are part of the same public learning experience.


### Learn how systems fail safely

[**Volume VII: The Reliability Field Guide**](OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) explains retries, idempotency, dead-letter handling and truthful user status. Its [Python lab](../projects/reliability-recovery-lab/) demonstrates the decisions with synthetic data and regression tests.

# THE OMNIMASTER HUMAN INTERFACE
### Volume VI | UI/UX engineering: designing for people, not merely for screens

**Cayelaem Jantjies · A practical account of how I build interfaces, learn from users and connect experience design to data and software engineering.**

[← GitHub profile](../README.md) · [My engineering story](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Engineering Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/)

---

> My work doesn't end when the data is correct. The person on the other end must be able to find it, understand it, trust it and act on it. That is why UI/UX development matters to me.

I have built dashboards, interfaces and application workflows across analytics and independent software projects. Working across SQL, APIs, React, reporting, mobile UI and authentication taught me that **usability is a system property**, not a layer of decoration added to finished code.

This volume explains how my thinking evolved from “make the information visible” to **“make the right action understandable, accessible and recoverable.”** I am involved in UI and UX development as part of my cross-stack work. I do not use that fact to invent a dedicated job title or claim that every usability hypothesis has already been validated with external research participants.

## Read by interest

| You want to know… | Start |
|---|---|
| How I became interested in interfaces beyond analytics | [01 · My UI/UX engineering journey](human-interface/01_MY_UX_JOURNEY.md) |
| What actually matters when people use software | [02 · Designing for real humans](human-interface/02_HUMAN_CENTRED_DESIGN.md) |
| How the ideas connect to products I build | [03 · Case studies and design reasoning](human-interface/03_UX_CASE_STUDIES.md) |
| How I build consistent, inclusive experiences | [04 · Design systems and accessibility](human-interface/04_DESIGN_SYSTEMS_AND_ACCESSIBILITY.md) |
| How I test whether an interface works | [05 · Usability research and measurement](human-interface/05_MEASURE_USABILITY.md) |
| How to practise and follow the same path | [06 · UI/UX workbook](human-interface/06_UX_WORKBOOK.md) |

## What changed my understanding of interface design

A technically correct dashboard can still make someone choose the wrong option. A successful API request can still leave a user wondering whether their change saved. An authentication screen can be secure but impossible to recover from. A visually impressive product can fail on narrow screens or with keyboard navigation.

I started paying attention to the entire journey, not simply the component.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    NEED["Person's goal"] --> UNDERSTAND["Understand their context"]
    UNDERSTAND --> TASK["Design the task flow"]
    TASK --> INTERFACE["Build a usable interface"]
    INTERFACE --> TEST["Observe, test and measure"]
    TEST --> IMPROVE["Repair the friction"]
    IMPROVE --> TASK
~~~

## The seven questions I ask about an interface

1. **Purpose:** what job does the person want done, and how urgent is it?
2. **Clarity:** can they tell what the system is showing and what to do next?
3. **Feedback:** what confirms success, saving, loading, failure or an irreversible action?
4. **Control:** can they undo, retry, correct or safely abandon the operation?
5. **Access:** does it work for different devices, abilities and technology constraints?
6. **Trust:** are data freshness, permissions, AI uncertainty and consequences explained?
7. **Evidence:** did we observe task success, or did we merely like the mock-up?

A UX designer learns the user's mental model. A UI developer makes the design behave predictably. A data engineer makes the state behind it correct. I enjoy the connections between all three.

## My project contexts

- **Enterprise dashboards:** metric labels, filter logic, chart clarity, performance and decision-making.
- **The Fixer:** ingestion setup, source previews, validation errors, role-aware workflows and administrative tools.
- **CABO Learning Hub:** distinct learner, parent and educator journeys, privacy, age-aware patterns and assessment feedback.
- **Mobile and responsive work:** narrow-width controls, readable charts, dark-mode behaviour, focus and platform differences.
- **OmniMaster portfolio and study room:** navigation, discoverability, interactive learning and a directly observable UX mistake: an HTML source link does not launch the experience.

Some of these are active product design or test workstreams, not proof of launched features or formal end-user study results. The chapters distinguish design intent, implementation and verified behaviour.

## The purpose of this volume

I want readers to be able to critique their own apps, not simply copy my colours. Each chapter includes a decision framework, examples and exercises. The workbook asks you to design a task, test it with people where possible, and improve it based on real observations.

**An interface should help a person succeed, not make them admire how hard the developer worked.**

[Start with my UI/UX journey →](human-interface/01_MY_UX_JOURNEY.md)


**Connecting user experience to backend reliability:** [Volume VII](OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) studies what people should see when processing is queued, retried, completed or awaiting manual review.

# THE OMNIMASTER FULL-STACK PLAYBOOK ### Frontend, backend, and everything that joins them **Cayelaem Jantjies · Engineer's field textbook · Edition 2026** [GitHub cover](../README.md) · [UI/UX development](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Volume V: Build with me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Read the full-stack book on the Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/OMNIMASTER_FULLSTACK_PLAYBOOK.md) --- > I don't call myself full-stack because I happen to know a frontend framework and a database. I use it to describe the work of turning a business need into a usable interface, a reliable API, a trustworthy data model, and a system people can operate. My foundation is Statistics and Data Science. Professional work across banking, manufacturing, research, broadcasting, agriculture and social-impact analytics gradually pushed me upstream and downstream: source SQL, data transformations, dashboards, APIs, backend services, React interfaces, testing, security and cloud delivery. I grew curious about **why the whole system behaves as it does**, not just which line of code renders the answer. This is a practical introduction to the separation between **frontend**, **backend**, and **full-stack integration**. It is for learners, recruiters and engineering reviewers. The exercises are synthetic and reproducible. They are not claims of production security certification or a transcript of private customer systems. ## Contents 1. [What is actually different?](#1-frontend-vs-backend-vs-full-stack) 2. [Frontend engineering: what people experience](#2-frontend-what-people-experience) 3. [Backend engineering: what the system guarantees](#3-backend-what-the-system-guarantees) 4. [A complete feature: from click to committed state](#4-trace-one-feature-across-the-stack) 5. [The third dimension: data and analytics engineering](#5-why-data-engineering-makes-me-a-different-full-stack-developer) 6. [Applied AI: how frontend and backend responsibilities differ](#6-applied-ai-across-the-stack) 7. [Testing and security: no layer gets a free pass](#7-testing-security-and-operations) 8. [UI/UX is a technical responsibility](#8-designing-for-people) 9. [My projects and the boundaries of my experience](#9-what-my-work-demonstrates) 10. [A study project you can build](#10-build-it-yourself) ## 1. Frontend vs backend vs full-stack Think of a booking, application or reporting workflow. Someone wants to find a record, understand it, change something and receive confirmation. **Frontend engineering** builds the experience: navigation, state, content, accessibility, visuals, charts, input and feedback. The frontend helps people understand and complete the task. **Backend engineering** builds trusted operations: identity, access rights, domain rules, data persistence, transactions, integrations, retries, auditing and failures. The backend ensures the action is *allowed and correctly performed*. **Full-stack engineering** connects them with explicit contracts and tests. It follows the user's intention through HTTP requests, policy checks, database writes and responses, and back to a meaningful interface. | Dimension | Frontend | Backend | Their shared responsibility | |---|---|---|---| | Typical execution | Browser/mobile runtime | Server, worker, container or managed runtime | A clear request/response boundary | | Primary focus | Usability and interaction | Correctness, data integrity and authorisation | Useful, reliable outcome | | Typical tools in my work | React, TypeScript, CSS, charts, browser testing | Node.js/TypeScript, APIs, SQL, PostgreSQL/MySQL, background services | Tests, typed contracts, logs, review | | Owns the visual loading state | Yes | Supplies the real operation state | Never show "complete" before completion | | Owns permissions | Useful navigation hints | **Actual enforcement** | Test denied routes end-to-end | | Owns form validation | Fast, helpful feedback | Authoritative rules | Consistent error contract | | Owns durable writes | No | Transactions and persistence | Idempotent UI-to-server actions | | Owns "real-time" meaning | Show freshness context | Source capture, processing and lag | Honest freshness expectations | | Can be tested independently | Components and browser | Units, HTTP and database | Full workflow / user acceptance | **Key distinction:** hiding the Admin button with CSS is not security. A frontend cannot decide for the server who may access a tenant's private data. ## 2. Frontend: what people experience When I build the frontend, my job is not just to make the interface attractive. I ask whether a person understands what the data says and can complete their goal with reasonable effort. ### What frontend developers actually build - **Information architecture:** page navigation, search, grouping and task prioritisation. - **Components and interaction:** reusable controls, forms, modals, tables, charts, filters and details. - **State management:** idle, loading, validating, queued, successful, partially successful, failed, cancelled and stale. - **API consumption:** data fetching, type-safe response handling, cache invalidation and optimistic updates where safe. - **Responsiveness:** layout and interaction across small phones, tablets and large screens. - **Accessibility:** semantic HTML, labels, contrast, keyboard focus, zoom, reduced motion and assistive technology. - **Performance:** fast first interaction, efficient rendering, small bundles and measured bottlenecks. - **Error recovery:** preserve useful input, explain errors and avoid confusing repeated submissions. - **Design quality:** hierarchy, consistency, typography and content that respects the user's mental model. ### Example: an import screen A person selects a source, tests credentials, previews data, validates records and synchronises them. These stages are not equivalent. The user should know when an action merely *checks*, when it *prepares*, and when it changes persistent state. A useful message is **"Preview complete: no records have been published."** A misleading message is **"All done!"** when the server only accepted an asynchronous job. This is why I connect frontend work with UX research. Read [Volume VI: The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md). ### Frontend sketch: model statuses explicitly ~~~tsx type ImportState = | { kind: "idle" } | { kind: "queued"; jobId: string } | { kind: "running"; processed: number } | { kind: "done"; accepted: number; rejected: number } | { kind: "failed"; message: string; safeToRetry: boolean }; function ImportNotice({ state }: { state: ImportState }) { switch (state.kind) { case "queued": return

Queued: {state.jobId}

; case "running": return

Processed {state.processed} rows.

; case "done": return

{state.accepted} imported; {state.rejected} rejected.

; case "failed": return

{state.message} {state.safeToRetry ? "Retry available." : "Check status first."}

; default: return

Choose a source to begin.

; } } ~~~ This illustrates frontend state modelling, not a finished production feature. Actual values must come from the backend, and content needs complete form and accessibility testing. ## 3. Backend: what the system guarantees When I work on the backend, I care about which operations can happen, whose data is involved, what is committed, and what a retry means. ### What backend developers actually build - **API design:** routes, response codes, input schemas, error contracts and versioning. - **Identity:** authentication, sessions, MFA and secure recovery policies. - **Authorisation:** role, operation, tenant and record scope enforced server-side. - **Domain logic:** business rules and valid state transitions, not rules scattered across browsers. - **Database design:** keys, constraints, transactions, indexes, migrations and data consistency. - **Integrations:** SQL sources, APIs, files, webhooks, third-party services and their failures. - **Background work:** job queues, retries, backoff, idempotency and dead-letter handling. - **Operations:** rate limits, observability, secure configuration, recovery and safe rollouts. - **Data governance:** audit trails, retention, provenance and access boundaries. ### HTTP statuses must mean something Imagine a user asks to synchronise data. | Response | Accurate meaning | Interface implication | |---|---|---| | **202 Accepted** | Server accepted work for processing | Show Queued, not Completed | | **200 OK** | The described synchronous operation succeeded | Show the actual result | | **400 Bad Request** | Invalid shape or input | Highlight correctable fields | | **401 Unauthorized** | No valid authentication | Prompt for sign-in safely | | **403 Forbidden** | Authenticated but not permitted | Deny without leaking data | | **409 Conflict** | State/version conflict | Ask user to reload or reconcile | | **429 Too Many Requests** | Request limit reached | Explain safe retry timing | | **5xx** | Unexpected service failure | Report uncertainty; don't assume write didn't happen | ### Backend sketch: enforce policy where it matters ~~~ts // Pseudocode showing responsibilities; not a working Fastify route. async function resolveException(request: RequestContext) { const actor = await authenticate(request); const input = validateResolution(request.body); const access = await authorise(actor, "exceptions.resolve", input.exceptionId); if (!access.allowed) return forbidden(); return db.transaction(async (tx) => { const row = await tx.selectExceptionForUpdate(input.exceptionId, access.tenantId); if (!row) return notFound(); if (row.status === "RESOLVED") return conflict("Already resolved"); await tx.markResolved(row.id, input.reason); await tx.writeAudit(actor.id, "exceptions.resolve", row.id); return success({ status: "RESOLVED" }); }); } ~~~ A transaction protects the combined state change inside the database. Real routes still need schema definitions, secure authentication, tenant lookup, consistent error handling, idempotency and integration tests. ## 4. Trace one feature across the stack ### Case: resolve a fictional delivery exception ~~~mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Person participant UI as React screen participant API as Authenticated API participant DB as PostgreSQL participant Jobs as Background worker Person->>UI: Select Resolve UI->>UI: Validate required reason UI->>API: POST /exceptions/{id}/resolve API->>API: Verify actor + tenant + permission API->>DB: Atomic state and audit update DB-->>API: Commit or conflict API-->>UI: Verified status or safe error UI-->>Person: Explain what actually happened API->>Jobs: Queue post-commit notification Jobs-->>API: Record outcome and retries ~~~ **Frontend responsibility:** make Resolve discoverable, require a meaningful reason, show a submitting state, prevent confusing duplicate clicks and explain success, conflict or unknown outcome. **Backend responsibility:** verify role and tenant, reject stale state, commit the change atomically, record the actor and protect the notification workflow against duplicates. **Full-stack responsibility:** write tests that start from user action and inspect backend truth. A button labelled "Resolved" must never be a substitute for the committed state. ### Common failure: the ambiguous network timeout The browser sends a request. The server commits. The response is lost. The frontend cannot safely assume failure and resubmit. The backend should provide a stable operation identifier or idempotency mechanism, plus a status endpoint. The frontend should say, **"We couldn't confirm the result. Check its status before retrying."** This is where real software engineering differs from demo tutorials. ## 5. Why data engineering makes me a different full-stack developer My foundation is not only frontend and backend code. I have worked with SQL, Power BI, DAX, Fabric-related analytics, ETL/ELT, source integration, modelling and performance across organisations and industries. That experience changes what I ask when building a product: 1. What is the authoritative event, and what does one row represent? 2. Can a join multiply a business amount? 3. How recent is the source, not merely the page render? 4. Can a changed record or delete be missed by an incremental pipeline? 5. Can access rules leak another market's or tenant's information? 6. Are the dashboard's numbers reproducible from source? A product becomes trustworthy when its **data grain, business semantics, API contract and interface wording** agree. ### Learn by building My [Data-to-Decision Platform](../projects/data-to-decision-platform/) demonstrates a synthetic source-event pipeline with versioning, atomic SQLite writes, current-state projection and tenant-specific metrics. It has no external identity layer or live CDC connection; it is an educational simulation. ## 6. Applied AI across the stack An AI feature is not a magic box attached to a button. Different layers own different risks. | Frontend / UX | Backend / data layer | |---|---| | Explain what the AI can and cannot do | Decide whether this task is permitted for the actor | | Show sources, uncertainty and review status | Retrieve approved source material under tenant/role scope | | Provide edit, reject, retry and human-review paths | Validate schema, source IDs, limits and content safety | | Avoid a confident-looking answer with no evidence | Log bounded decisions, costs, failures and provenance | | Preserve user control | Apply deterministic state transitions; no silent consequential writes | ### An education example A teacher asks AI to suggest feedback on a fictional learner answer. The frontend should make the output recognisable as a suggestion, show the relevant rubric and source and offer a deliberate review action. The backend should verify educator access, retrieve only the permitted learner and rubric, bound provider use, validate scoring constraints and require explicit human approval before an official grade changes. My [Offline AI Output Evaluation Lab](../projects/ai-output-evaluation/) teaches a narrow extractive-evidence contract. It does **not** prove semantic truth, privacy compliance or production-level AI reliability. ## 7. Testing, security and operations A meaningful "done" depends on the layer. | Test class | Frontend evidence | Backend evidence | End-to-end question | |---|---|---|---| | Unit | Correct component state | Business-rule invariant | Are the parts internally coherent? | | Integration | Correct API decoding | Actual database operation | Did they agree on schema and semantics? | | Browser | User completes the task | Role/tenant denial is enforced | Does the user journey work? | | Accessibility | Focus, labels, reflow, screen reader | Useful error information | Can different people understand and recover? | | Security | No secrets or false trust assumptions | Auth, MFA, IDOR, input, SSRF and least privilege | Does an attacker bypass the intended boundary? | | Reliability | Honest queued/failed states | Retry, checkpoint, rollback and alerting | What happens when a dependency fails? | | Release | UI assets on intended version | Migration and config on intended version | Did this exact commit pass the right gates? | A green unit suite is useful, but it does not prove a real deploy, accessibility compliance or authorisation on every route. ## 8. Designing for people is engineering UI/UX development matters because a system's job is not just to compute the right output. It must help people *use* the output. The questions I now ask about an interface are practical: can someone find the task, understand the meaning, tell whether something saved, recover when it fails, use the screen on a phone and know what happens to their information? One lesson arrived directly from this portfolio: the "Interactive Study Room" link initially opened an **HTML source file in GitHub** instead of the actual experience. The code was there, but the person could not use it. Fixing the destination was a usability improvement, not a CSS improvement. [Volume VI: The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) contains full chapters on task design, accessibility, design systems, user research and practical UX exercises. ## 9. What my work demonstrates | Workstream | Frontend or UX work | Backend / data work | Status boundary | |---|---|---|---| | Enterprise BI engagements | Dashboards, reporting UX, semantic labels and visual performance | SQL modelling, transformations, metric definitions and data reconciliation | Historical professional work, proprietary source | | The Fixer / NewChanges | Source previews, admin workflows, responsive/dashboard interfaces | TypeScript/Fastify APIs, PostgreSQL, imports, auth/MFA workstreams, tests | Public code with active gates; not a blanket production-readiness claim | | CABO Learning Hub | Learner, teacher, guardian and admin journeys; assessments and mobile design | Identity, institutional roles, records, AI routing and validation | Active product development; no claimed government rollout | | Financial and HR prototypes | Forms, review flows, reporting and role-aware UX | Transaction rules, auditability, data permissions and domain models | Prototypes/staging with project-specific limitations | | OmniMaster Study Room | Interactive questions, progress, navigation and accessible controls | Hosted delivery and test checks; browser-local progress | Live teaching product; final manual QA remains separate | I am strongest in data engineering, BI/analytics and full-stack application delivery, with growing exposure to cloud/platform operations, security engineering, mobile and AI. **My ability to contribute across much of software-oriented IT is not a claim to be an expert in every specialist niche. Hardware engineering and physical device repair are not my area of focus.** ## 10. Build it yourself: the exception tracker Create a fictional two-tenant exception workflow. Build only one complete path first. **Step A: define the data.** One exception has a stable ID, tenant, status, assigned actor, created timestamp and resolution history. **Step B: design the frontend.** A list, detail page and Resolve action with loading, confirmation, conflict and error states. Test keyboard navigation and a narrow mobile viewport. **Step C: design the backend.** Use an authenticated API, role/tenant checks, valid state transitions, transaction/audit consistency, and an idempotency strategy. **Step D: prove denial.** Try a wrong-tenant ID, a revoked session and a duplicate resolution attempt. Verify no unauthorised state change or leakage. **Step E: make failure understandable.** Disconnect the browser after request submission. Does the frontend promise a retry it cannot justify? Does the backend expose enough state to reconcile what happened? **Step F: document the boundary.** Write a README saying what was implemented, what was tested and what is missing before real deployment. ### Five review questions 1. What must happen on the server even if the browser lies? 2. How does a frontend distinguish "queued" from "done"? 3. Why does a transaction matter for state change plus audit? 4. What happens to the user if a request commits but the response disappears? 5. Which tests prove a feature, and which merely prove a toy component? **The most interesting full-stack skill is not knowing every syntax rule. It is knowing which part of the system owns the truth, how the layers cooperate and what a real person experiences when something goes wrong.** --- **Explore further:** [The OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Engineering Field Guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Build With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [UI/UX Development](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) *Educational text written as a first-person field guide. Examples are synthetic. Private client information is intentionally excluded.* **The next lesson:** [Volume VII · Reliability and Recovery](OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) shows why a frontend's message must reflect actual background-job state, and how the backend implements retries and failure recovery.

# THE OMNIMASTER RELIABILITY FIELD GUIDE
### Volume VII | What happens after everything goes wrong?

**Cayelaem Jantjies · Reliability engineering, truthful UX, retries and recovery**

[The public Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) · [My technical handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Build the reliability lab](../projects/reliability-recovery-lab/)

---

> Reliable engineering isn't only making the happy path fast. It's explaining exactly what happened when the happy path didn't happen.

I came into technology through statistics, data, reporting and the challenge of making operational decisions trustworthy. As I moved deeper into APIs, databases, automations, cloud delivery and UI/UX development, I learned that the critical question is often **"What if the action only partly succeeded?"**

A failed job, lost response, repeated payment request, slow CDC source or inconsistent status message can make an otherwise elegant product misleading. This volume teaches how to reason about those boundaries.

## Read the five chapters

| Chapter | What you will understand | Hands-on exercise |
|---|---|---|
| [01 · A job is a contract](reliability/01_JOBS_AND_STATE.md) | The difference between received, queued, running, retried, done and dead | Define a finite state machine |
| [02 · Retries without chaos](reliability/02_RETRIES_AND_IDEMPOTENCY.md) | At-least-once delivery, backoff, duplicate effects and idempotency keys | Replay a synthetic job |
| [03 · Dead letters and recovery](reliability/03_DEAD_LETTERS_AND_RECONCILIATION.md) | Why failed items need ownership and safe recovery | Force three failures, then requeue |
| [04 · Make failure understandable](reliability/04_STATUS_UX_AND_OPERATIONS.md) | Frontend status, user trust, operational observability and accessible feedback | Design a truthful job timeline |
| [05 · Beyond a local simulation](reliability/05_PRODUCTION_BOUNDARIES.md) | Transactions, distributed failure, outbox/inbox, source positions and release gates | Write a production upgrade proposal |

## The executable lab

**[Open the OmniMaster Reliability & Recovery Lab](../projects/reliability-recovery-lab/)**.

~~~bash
cd projects/reliability-recovery-lab
python cli.py
python -m unittest discover -v
~~~

The code runs in-memory SQLite with no network, cloud services, accounts, keys or real customer data. It uses synthetic tenants and a simulated integer clock.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    UI["Person requests action"] --> API["Backend accepts job"]
    API --> PEND["PENDING"]
    PEND --> RUN{"Attempt succeeds?"}
    RUN -->|"No, more attempts"| RETRY["RETRY with backoff"]
    RETRY --> RUN
    RUN -->|"No, limit reached"| DEAD["DEAD: operator decision"]
    RUN -->|"Yes"| DONE["DONE with local audit"]
    DEAD --> RECOVER["Manual requeue or safe resolution"]
    RECOVER --> RUN
    PEND -.-> STATUS["Frontend: Queued, not Completed"]
    RETRY -.-> STATUS
    DEAD -.-> STATUS
    DONE -.-> STATUS
~~~

## The example outcome

Two wholly fictional jobs are submitted.

- `tenant-beta` completes at tick 0.
- `tenant-alpha` encounters `source_unavailable` twice, at ticks 0 and 2.
- At tick 6, alpha completes. The local event log records each transition.
- If alpha had failed again, it would enter `DEAD`, where a person must decide whether to requeue it.

**"Effect committed" in this project means an inserted row in one local SQLite database.** It is not a bank payment, a sent email or a successful external service call.

## Why this matters to the person using the software

Consider a page showing **"Upload completed"** when the backend has merely accepted a task. If the source later fails, that message was wrong. The backend's job state and the frontend's language must agree.

The question is not just whether there is a spinner. It is whether someone knows if a task was performed, may still finish, failed safely, needs attention or may already have caused an external effect.

That is the connection between **backend engineering and human-centred UX** I want people to learn.

## The lessons from my own engineering practice

Data pipelines taught me to ask whether records actually reached their destination. Full-stack product work taught me to ask which action was authorised, committed and auditable. Security reviews taught me that a passing test only proves what that test observed. UI development taught me to care about how the result is explained to the person waiting for it.

My professional and independent projects include reporting, integration and security workstreams, but this teaching lab is deliberately fictional. It does not reproduce proprietary operational processes or establish the production maturity of The Fixer or any other live system.

## Where this fits in the library

[Volume III · The Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) teaches core methods. [Volume V · Build With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) builds a synthetic event-to-metric pipeline. [Volume VI · The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) studies usability and accessible design. [The Frontend / Backend Playbook](OMNIMASTER_FULLSTACK_PLAYBOOK.md) explains ownership across application layers.

**Volume VII connects all four through failure and recovery.**

# Reliability Chapter 01 | A job is a contract

[← Volume VII](../OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Retry safely →](02_RETRIES_AND_IDEMPOTENCY.md)

## The distinction that saves support tickets

When a person starts an operation, **receiving a request is not the same as finishing the work**. The backend may validate and enqueue the task while an independent worker does the actual processing later.

For a frontend, this distinction changes every status label and every promise made to a user.

## Draw the state machine first

| State | What it means in the teaching lab | What the interface may truthfully say |
|---|---|---|
| `PENDING` | Accepted, waiting for its first due attempt | "Queued for processing" |
| `RETRY` | Previous attempt failed; new attempt scheduled | "We're retrying. No success confirmed yet." |
| `DONE` | Local simulated effect, job update and audit committed | "Finished in the teaching simulator" |
| `DEAD` | Automatic attempt limit reached | "We couldn't complete the task. Review is needed." |

Real systems may need more states: `RUNNING`, `CANCELLED`, `PARTIAL`, `UNKNOWN`, `WAITING_FOR_APPROVAL`. A state machine should model the actual business guarantees rather than copy a fashionable queue vocabulary.

## See it in code

Open [reliability.py](../../projects/reliability-recovery-lab/reliability.py) and inspect the `jobs` table. The columns `status`, `attempts`, `next_due` and `last_error` make the decision to retry or stop observable.

~~~bash
cd projects/reliability-recovery-lab
python cli.py
~~~

The demonstration has two fictional tenants. Beta succeeds immediately. Alpha fails twice before succeeding. The events are deterministic and make no network requests.

## A common frontend mistake

The API returns `202 Accepted`. A UI immediately displays a permanent green **Completed** badge.

That is a usability defect and a correctness defect: the backend only accepted work; completion remains unknown.

The safer flow is:

~~~text
Submit task
  -> 202 Accepted, operation ID
  -> Show "Queued"
  -> Poll/subscribe to an authorised status endpoint
  -> Show "Processing", "Retrying", "Needs review" or "Done"
  -> Provide an appropriate next action
~~~

The teaching lab does not implement HTTP. You would need a verified session, tenant-derived scope, and a status endpoint before exposing these records.

## Practical task

Write down the exact allowed transitions: PENDING → RETRY, RETRY → DONE, RETRY → DEAD, DEAD → manually requeued. Then identify which transitions must be forbidden, such as marking a dead job as done without a new attempt.

## Review checklist

- Is every status name linked to an actual backend condition?
- Can the frontend display uncertainty rather than invent completion?
- Is a user's tenant derived from authenticated identity, not a query parameter?
- Can operations staff distinguish a permanent failure from a temporary delay?
- Does a retry change the status and preserve the previous error?

**Pass criterion:** a non-technical person can correctly interpret every displayed state and know when to retry, wait or seek help.

[Next: Retry safely →](02_RETRIES_AND_IDEMPOTENCY.md)

# Reliability Chapter 02 | Retry without causing the problem twice

[← Job contracts](01_JOBS_AND_STATE.md) · [Volume VII](../OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Dead letters →](03_DEAD_LETTERS_AND_RECONCILIATION.md)

## The uncomfortable truth about retries

A network timeout might mean an action did not happen, **or** that the action happened and its response was lost. Retrying blindly can duplicate work, notifications, imports or payments.

This matters in the full-stack workflow because the browser only sees the outcome it received, not necessarily the server's actual state.

## Why idempotency is useful

**Idempotency** means repeating the same logical operation doesn't create additional unintended effects. In the teaching lab, the job has a stable `job_id` and an `effect_key`.

- Re-submitting the same job ID with identical data is a harmless replay.
- Reusing the same job ID with different data fails closed.
- Multiple jobs using the same effect key and **same** tenant/payload produce a single local effect.
- Reusing an effect key with different payload or across tenants is rejected.

The code demonstrates these guarantees in **one local SQLite database**. It does not provide exactly-once delivery to an email, payment gateway or remote data warehouse.

## Bounded backoff

Run the example:

~~~bash
cd projects/reliability-recovery-lab
python cli.py
~~~

The simulated retry schedule uses `min(8, 2 × 2^(attempt−1))` ticks. The first failure waits two ticks; the second waits four; the cap is eight. Automatic processing stops after three failures.

| Attempt | At simulated tick | Outcome | Next action |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | Source unavailable | Retry at tick 2 |
| 2 | 2 | Source unavailable | Retry at tick 6 |
| 3 | 6 | Successful local effect | Commit DONE and audit |

This is **deterministic** educational backoff without jitter. Real systems should evaluate jitter, rate limits, source retry-after instructions, bounded queue pressure and whether an error is transient at all.

## Why the database transaction matters

In `run_due()`, the local effect row, job state and audit entry are changed together inside one SQLite transaction. If those local writes fail, the database can roll them back.

But imagine a real external service accepted a request before SQLite saved the result. The external effect **cannot be undone** by a local database rollback. You need a delivery contract that accounts for this, often involving an outbox/inbox, external idempotency key and reconciliation.

## Exercise: duplicate work

1. Create two fictional jobs with the same effect key, tenant and payload.
2. Run due work. Confirm only one local effect row exists.
3. Change one payload but reuse the key. Confirm the simulator rejects it.
4. Write a three-sentence explanation of what would be different if the effect were a real email or payment.

## Test the negative path

Read [test_reliability.py](../../projects/reliability-recovery-lab/test_reliability.py). The suite checks duplicate suppression, conflicting key reuse, retry timing and absence of unintended local effects.

**Pass criterion:** you can explain the distinction between **at-least-once delivery**, **idempotent processing** and a true external exactly-once guarantee without treating them as synonyms.

[Next: Dead letters and recovery →](03_DEAD_LETTERS_AND_RECONCILIATION.md)

# Reliability Chapter 03 | Dead letters, evidence and recovery

[← Safe retries](02_RETRIES_AND_IDEMPOTENCY.md) · [Volume VII](../OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Reliable UX →](04_STATUS_UX_AND_OPERATIONS.md)

## When automatic retries must stop

A system that retries forever can turn one bad event into an operational incident. It consumes resources, floods logs, pressures the dependency and leaves users waiting for something that will never happen.

The **dead-letter state** separates automatic processing from deliberate human review.

In this synthetic lab, `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3`. A third failed attempt sets the status to `DEAD`, records `last_error` and an audit transition, and does not insert any local effect.

## A responsible recovery workflow

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    FAIL["Attempt fails"] --> N{"Attempt limit reached?"}
    N -->|"No"| RETRY["Schedule safe retry"]
    N -->|"Yes"| DEAD["DEAD: needs operator review"]
    DEAD --> CHECK["Inspect cause and external effects"]
    CHECK --> DECIDE{"Safe to replay?"}
    DECIDE -->|"Yes"| RECOVER["Requeue with audit record"]
    DECIDE -->|"No"| RESOLVE["Resolve by documented alternative"]
    RECOVER --> TEST["Verify outcome and reconcile"]
~~~

The lab's `requeue_dead(job_id,tenant,now)` method allows a dead fictional job to be requeued, resetting the attempt count and adding a `MANUAL_REQUEUE` entry.

It rejects attempts to requeue a job in the wrong tenant, one that is pending or one already completed.

## Where the user interface matters

An operator needs more than a generic `Failed` label. Show the safe error category, last attempt, how many attempts ran, whether any effect might already have occurred, whether another attempt is automatic, and the appropriate next action.

A real product may need an incident ID, business impact, escalation level, permission-based requeue and a peer approval for consequential actions.

## Practice

Using a disposable Python session:

~~~python
from reliability import ReliabilityLab

with ReliabilityLab() as lab:
    lab.submit("job-demo", "tenant-demo", "effect-demo", {"message": "fictional only"})
    faults = {("job-demo", n): "source_unavailable" for n in (1, 2, 3)}
    for tick in (0, 2, 6):
        lab.run_due(tick, faults)

    assert lab.jobs_for("tenant-demo")[0]["status"] == "DEAD"
    assert lab.effects_for("tenant-demo") == []
    lab.requeue_dead("job-demo", "tenant-demo", 20)
    lab.run_due(20)
    assert lab.jobs_for("tenant-demo")[0]["status"] == "DONE"
~~~

## A cautious technical note

The SQLite database here is **in-memory and disposable**. Its history is an audit *demonstration*, not a durable production audit trail. It does not implement real operational approvals, external effect reconciliation or incident recovery.

For real systems, document retention, immutable history requirements, notification/alert routing and the conditions under which an item is safe to requeue.

## Review questions

1. What should a system do with a permanently malformed record?
2. How do you distinguish a temporary dependency failure from a business-rule violation?
3. What evidence do you require before a human presses Requeue?
4. How can you tell whether an external effect occurred before a crash?
5. When should an item be marked Resolved rather than attempted again?

**Pass criterion:** you can write a safe operator playbook with a reason for every manual action.

# Reliability Chapter 04 | Truthful frontend status and operational UX [← Dead letters](03_DEAD_LETTERS_AND_RECONCILIATION.md) · [Volume VII](../OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Production boundaries →](05_PRODUCTION_BOUNDARIES.md) ## A backend failure becomes a human experience I have learned that an interface can be technically valid and still lie to its user. The common pattern is simple: an action is queued, a network response is late, and the UI announces success because it received *something*. In a reliable product, **the language of the interface must correspond to a genuine system state**. ## Frontend status contract | Backend truth | Avoid saying | Say something useful instead | |---|---|---| | Queued but not attempted | "Completed" | "Your task has been queued" | | In progress | "Saved" | "Processing; you can check its status here" | | Retry scheduled | "Failed" without context | "We're retrying after a temporary problem" | | Automatic retries exhausted | "Try again" as if risk-free | "This needs review before another attempt" | | Local effect committed | "Everything sent" when external outcome unknown | "Local processing finished; delivery confirmation pending" | | Result unknown after timeout | "Nothing happened" | "We couldn't confirm the result; check status before retrying" | Every sample message must be backed by real behaviour before it is used in a production product. ## A UI component is a state machine in disguise The frontend needs a typed status contract, accessible labels, focus management and careful error recovery. A status view could show: ~~~tsx type JobStatus = | { state: "queued"; id: string } | { state: "retrying"; attempt: number; nextCheckAt: string } | { state: "done"; completedAt: string } | { state: "needs_review"; incidentId: string } | { state: "unknown"; id: string }; function JobNotice({ job }: { job: JobStatus }) { switch (job.state) { case "queued": return

Queued. Reference {job.id}.

; case "retrying": return

Attempt {job.attempt} failed; retry planned.

; case "done": return

Processing finished at {job.completedAt}.

; case "needs_review": return

Review required. Case {job.incidentId}.

; case "unknown": return

Outcome not confirmed. Check reference {job.id}.

; } } ~~~ This is a **teaching fragment**, not a full authenticated React application. In a real system, UI status must be fetched from a backend endpoint authorised for the user's verified identity and tenant. ## Reliability is also information architecture A frustrated user should not have to understand message brokers, transaction logs or process IDs. They need to know whether to **wait, retry, review, cancel or contact support**. An operator needs richer detail: attempt history, failure category, correlation ID, source state, last successful checkpoint, incident owner and safe remediation options. The two interfaces serve different people and should not simply render the same raw JSON. ## How I would validate the experience 1. Give a participant a fictional task and deliberately make the source fail. 2. Ask them to interpret the status without explaining the system. 3. Observe whether they click Retry repeatedly or wait when appropriate. 4. Test a lost response after a committed action. 5. Verify keyboard access, screen-reader announcements and mobile layout. 6. Compare every displayed promise with the actual backend state. This is a proposed usability method, not a claim that a formal study has already been completed. ## What metrics would help? | Metric | Why it matters | |---|---| | Oldest due job age | Identifies backlog and stalled work | | Retry count by error category | Distinguishes dependency instability from invalid input | | Dead-letter count and age | Reveals tasks needing human attention | | Time to verified completion | Connects processing performance to user expectation | | Status uncertainty rate | Measures lost/ambiguous outcomes | | Cross-tenant denial tests | Confirms that status visibility is not a data leak | Avoid collecting sensitive content as a shortcut for observability. Structured, minimal event metadata is usually preferable. **Pass criterion:** a person knows what the system has actually completed and how they should proceed without understanding the infrastructure. # Reliability Chapter 05 | From a local retry toy to real operations

[← Status UX](04_STATUS_UX_AND_OPERATIONS.md) · [Volume VII](../OMNIMASTER_RELIABILITY_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Back to the Academy](../OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md)

## Don't confuse deterministic tests with distributed guarantees

The runnable lab is valuable because you can inspect every decision and reproduce every failure. That is not the same as proving a production system will recover from worker crashes, network partitions, source replays or downstream outages.

Here is the gap a responsible engineer should make explicit.

| Dimension | Local teaching lab | Production design requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | In-memory SQLite | Durable storage, backups, HA and restore rehearsal |
| Work scheduling | Simulated integer clock | Real-time scheduling, visibility timeout and clock skew |
| Worker concurrency | One process | Multiple workers, claim/lease semantics and bounded parallelism |
| Delivery semantics | Deterministic local effect | Real source acknowledgements and idempotent external effects |
| Identity | Tenant parameter only | Authenticated actor, operation permission and server-derived tenant |
| Observability | Local audit table | Structured logs, metrics, alerts, tracing, retention and owner |
| Requeue | Direct method call | Operator authentication, approval, audit and duplicate-effect reconciliation |
| Traffic | A handful of fictional jobs | Load and saturation testing, capacity budgets and backpressure |
| Failure recovery | Scripted temporary failures | Process crash, timeout, partial write, external outage and rollback |
| Release | Local tests | Staging, CI, canary/gradual rollout and rollback plan |

## The failure window that matters most

Imagine an API call to send a message succeeds. The worker crashes before its local database records that outcome.

On restart, the job is still pending. A blind retry might send the message twice. **Local SQL transactions cannot roll back an already-committed external HTTP side effect.**

Possible controls include stable external idempotency keys, durable outbox/inbox records, reconciliation from provider receipts and state machines that preserve unknown outcomes. None is a universal magic fix; they must fit the target service's semantics.

## A safe engineering progression

**Stage 1. Correct local state:** source contracts, idempotency tests, bounded retries and visible failures.

**Stage 2. Durable persistence:** use a disposable database file or container, test restart, restore, schema migration and corruption detection.

**Stage 3. Real worker coordination:** introduce claims/leases and concurrent consumers in a local test environment. Test a worker that loses its lease midway through work.

**Stage 4. External synthetic integration:** use a mock or disposable downstream service. Inject timeouts both before and after the service commits.

**Stage 5. Security and tenant isolation:** enforce verified identity at HTTP boundaries, roles, tenant membership, least privilege and audit trails; test tampered identifiers.

**Stage 6. Operational proof:** implement dashboards, error budgets, alerts, a dead-letter response playbook, release gates and rollback.

## Release review questions

- Did the destination effect actually happen, or only local state update?
- What evidence survives a crash between the two operations?
- Can a duplicate source event produce a second real-world effect?
- Can workers concurrently claim the same job?
- Can a caller inspect or requeue another tenant's job?
- What happens during an hour-long downstream outage?
- Which states can be safely retried and which need human approval?
- Can a deploy be reverted without losing acknowledged jobs?
- Does the UI distinguish accepted, processing, confirmed and unknown?

## Your capstone assignment

Design a **fictional scheduled reporting system**. It processes a CSV of synthetic metrics and posts a mock notification. Specify the queue, job ID, idempotency key, maximum attempts, retry rules, manual review policy, status API, test matrix, source-of-truth and operations checklist.

Then implement only the smallest version that proves one risk. Your documentation should say precisely what it cannot yet guarantee.

I care about reliability because it connects all the layers I enjoy: SQL and source truth, backend business rules, DevSecOps, full-stack user experiences and the responsibility to explain a system honestly.

**The goal is not to avoid every failure. The goal is to make failure bounded, observable, recoverable and understandable.**
